https://www.thetimes.com/culture/photogr.title: This month in the Times photographic archive: August 2021
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/photogr.text:
The ongoing consequences of the withdrawal of American forces saw Afghanistan dominate the headlines this month.
Key districts fell into the clutches of the Taliban, as the Afghan army collapsed at an alarming rate, surprising western forces still based in Kabul. President Ghani fled by helicopter hours before the Taliban seized control of the presidential palace. Chaotic scenes ensued over the coming days in Kabul as US, British and other western allies scrambled to evacuate their citizens and diplomatic staff. Thousands of Afghans who had worked alongside western forces applied for emergency evacuation, and many more risked their lives in tragic scenes attempting to board planes by any means.
Afghanistan has a legacy of war, occupation and resistance stretching back many decades. Researching the archive for images of past conflicts we digitised a Sunday Times shoot by Duncan Baxter taken in 1982, the third year of Russian occupation in the Soviet-Afghan war, while on assignment with Simon Winchester in the Afghan hills.
The mujahidin were backed with American funds and weaponry in a proxy for the Cold War which lasted nine years and eventually saw the Soviet Union defeated and the fall of its communist Afghan government.
However, stability was not achieved and a further civil war led to the rise of the Taliban, who seized power in 1996.
Gurkha veterans have fought for proper recognition from the UK for their efforts for the British Army for years, with the actress Joanna Lumley one of their fiercest supporters. In London this month several went on hunger strike for 13 days outside Downing Street, demanding parity of their pensions with other veterans who retired before 1997.
The protests only ended when the Ministry of Defence agreed to meet the Nepalese ambassador for talks. Lumley said that ministers “cannot praise our veterans to the high heavens when it suits them, but ignore them and condemn them to poverty when it doesn’t”.
Searching for historical images of Gurkhas uncovered these two glass plate negatives featuring a Gurkha winner of the Victoria Cross, and two Punjabi Indian recipients, highlighting the parity and fairness at issue this month.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change published its landmark scientific report in August documenting the consequences of climate change. The headlines led with their ominous declaration that this should be a “code red for humanity”. The report outlines the expected growth in temperatures of 1.5C within two decades and breaching it by 2040 — even if the world rapidly reduces its carbon emissions.
Just weeks after the report, the environmental activist group Extinction Rebellion returned to the streets of London, erecting a 13ft-high pink table near Leicester Square with “Come To The Table” written on it. A search for early environmental activism discovered an anti-pollution protest in London from 1971. The captions describe a “carnival atmosphere”, but policing was more rigorous.
International cat day has been celebrated on August 8 each year after being created by the International Fund for Animal Welfare. We searched the archives for images to illustrate the concept from an earlier time.
Here the “Milk Bar” is open in the first image taken at Sadler’s Wells theatre in London in 1956. Auditions were being held for a cat to star in “School for Fathers”. A wonderfully playful image shows the cats getting signed in by the hopeful owners as they are treated to free milk. The role demanded a cat with “dignity and poise” to stand on a 10ft wall while the singers and orchestra play, a sardine awaits the winning cat, their reward for each performance on the stage.
Another image is taken in a real bar, the Unicorn pub in Shoreditch owned by publican Harold Smith. If you look closely you can see Minnie the owner’s cat in the bottom left corner, his paw on the bar grabbing some coins as the gentlemen enjoy a pint and a smoke. As the caption describes he is certainly a cat to watch “quick as a flash his paw will cover your change on the bar and Minnie has another coin in the kitty”.
In the interest of balance in the pet loving world it was also International Dog Day on 26th August, providing us with an excuse to browse the collection we hold on man’s best friend.
We are in the process of digitising our extensive collection of civil aviation images and the sad story of the Saunders-Roe SR 45 Princess seemed like an interesting place to start.
The Air Ministry was planning for post-war civil aviation as the Second World War went on, and one of its chosen designs was this flying boat, designed to carry 100 passengers across the Atlantic. Time photographers recorded the five-year construction of the SR 45 on the Isle of Wight, but by the time it flew in 1952 advances in aircraft design had already rendered it obsolete.
August was a busy month in the sporting calendar with the Olympics, football being played in full stadiums and the return of the Henley Regatta.
The regatta has been famous for its strict dress code, but updated it this year to allow women to wear trousers for the first time in its 182 years — though skirt hemlines still had to be below the knee.
This early colour shot from 1937 beautifully illustrates the historic event, complete with full-length summer dresses.
The Olympics concluded in August with Great Britain making a record haul of 65 medals. Tom Daley excelled in the diving, finally achieving a lifetime ambition winning his gold medal alongside Matty Lee in the 10m synchro platform.
Photographing sporting events such as the diving which are over in the blink of an eye has become a much easier task for the modern press photographer with huge leaps in digital camera technology and automated remote control triggers.
We discovered a stunning set of glass plate negatives taken of the Highgate diving club at the Seymour Place baths in 1951. The photographer Charles Trusler was working within the strict limits of glass plate negatives and a press camera assisted by a harsh flash bulb, making the photographs even more extraordinary. The margin for error was incredibly thin.
Brentford made a triumphant return to top flight football as they kicked off the new premier league season with a victory over Arsenal.
A charming set of images were scanned this month of the Brentford squad preparing for the coming season in August 1950 at Griffin Park, their home stadium until last year.
Charlie Watts, the legendary drummer of The Rolling Stones died this month aged 80.
The Sunday Times photographer Kevin Brodie managed to get into the Stones’ hotel room with the band when they played a gig in Birmingham in 1964, even having breakfast with them. For some reason, the images were never published in the paper.
Despite Watts’s famous grumbles about the fame and his bafflement at the excesses of the rock and roll lifestyle, he was regarded as the heartbeat of the band. Losing such a talismanic figure could well mark the end of one of the greatest ever rock and roll bands.

image.caption: The journalist Simon Winchester poses with guerrilla fighters

Many of the mujahidin were Hazara tribesmen, Shia Muslims, proud of their fighting heritage: “We are the heirs of Genghis Khan. We kill Russians.” It is not known whether this is a family pose of a father with his daughters — and a grenade launcher and assault rifle

Gurkha Rifleman Bhanbhagta Gurung, pictured in October, 1945, won the Victoria Cross for his actions in Burma in August that year, exposing himself to fire to kill a sniper, then singlehandedly clearing four foxholes and killing their occupants with grenades and his kukri while under machinegun fire. He then attacked and took the machinegun bunker, manned it and beat off an enemy counterattack

Bhanbhagta Gurung shows his kukri to Corporal Gian Singh, left, who won his VC on the advance through Burma in February 1945, single-handedly attacking and clearing machinegun emplacements in foxholes and an anti-tank emplacement despite being badly wounded, and Sergeant Umrao Singh. The sergeant fought off three attacks on his field gun detachment in December 1944, despite being wounded by two grenades and eventually resorting to hand-to-hand combat using an iron rod before being overcome
Modern protesters erected a huge pink table in London. Their predecessors tried to use balloons, flowers and singing to block Oxford Street in 1971
Modern policing, as far as possible, emphasises negotiation — police in 1971 were prepared to manhandle a protester out of the way

The “milk bar” was set up for cats brought in by their owners for auditions at Sadler’s Wells theatre in London in 1956. Twenty five cats turned up for a role which required “dignity and poise” — and standing on a wall as the cast of School for Fathers sang below them
A close look at the lower left of the picture shows Minnie, the cat owned by Harold Smith, the publican of the Unicorn in Shoreditch in 1952. Minnie was known for grabbing coins off the bar
A young boy — name unknown — brings his British bulldog to the Alldogs dog beauty parlour in 1954
It’s quite hard to beat a bulldog pulling a face at having its fur shampooed and scalp massaged
The installation of a Bristol Proteus engine in the massive flying boat at the factory in East Cowes on the Isle of Wight in February 1951. It needed six of them to fly
The first prototype of the SR45 Princess flying boat, registration G-ALUN, was brought out of its factory hangar for viewing at the end of October, 1951
The chief test pilot Geoffrey Tyson took the controls for maiden flight of the SR45 in August, 1952
London and Glasgow fight it out to the finish at the Henley Regatta in 1937
Peter Elliott from Highgate diving club in a reverse pixie dive from the 3m springboard during a competition against Nautique Havrais of France in 1951
Yoaan Raanan from the Highgate club performs a flying somersault dive from the 3m board
​​The Brentford manager Jackie Gibbons with his squad in 1950, including — third from right — a young Jimmy Hill
The corrugated roof of the Griffin Park stand looms behind Johnny Paton, Hill, Bill Dare and Bill Pointon. The club were in the Second Division, having been relegated in 1947
Brian Jones, Mick Jagger, Charlie Watts and Keith Richards, far right, laugh as bass player Bill Wyman mugs in their room at the Grand Hotel in Birmingham in 1964
The famously grumpy Charlie Watts looking relaxed and happy in the early days
These mujahidin guerillas were pictured in the hills of Afghanistan between raids on the regular Afghan army and occupying Soviet troops in 1982

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/offi.title: Officers mobilised as Extinction Rebellion protests kick off in Trafalgar Square
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/offi.text:
Extinction Rebellion protesters have brought part of London’s West End to a standstill as police warned that the group’s actions would divert resources and hinder efforts to tackle violent crime.
Up to 1,000 activists marched from Trafalgar Square to Covent Garden where they set up a blockade.
Protesters erected a 13ft-high pink table at a junction near Leicester Square Tube station with “Come To The Table” written on it.
It is the first site to be blockaded and occupied by the group this year. It is reminiscent of the pink boat that protesters erected at Oxford Circus during demonstrations in April 2019.
Protesters quickly climbed on top of the table, which is equipped with sleeping quarters and areas where they can lock themselves in.
Others lay on the ground with their arms encased in a suitcase packed with concrete, as a means of preventing police from dispersing the protest.
Marion Malcher, 66, was among those lying in middle of Cranbourn Street with her arm in a suitcase. She said this was her first time locking on. “It’s certainly quite the experience,” she said.
The climate change activists claimed last week that thousands would take part in what it said would be two weeks of protests mainly targeting the City of London.
Police officers lined Whitehall, guarding the entrances to government departments. Territorial Support Group vans were also on hand. The unit is typically deployed to deal with major incidents such as terror attacks and riots.
The protest began with activists saying a Creole prayer to mark the 230th anniversary of the Haitian revolution that saw slaves overthrow French colonial rule.
Drawing comparisons between colonial rule and the climate crisis, a speaker told demonstrators: “Colonisers have always feared the indigenous people for their ability to commune with nature. Let us put an end to that global system of domination and set yourselves free.”
Activists from Animal Rebellion, an animal welfare offshoot of Extinction Rebellion (XR), were among the demonstrators.
Gail Bradbrook, co-founder of XR, told the crowd that nine activists were in police custody after members of the group scaled the Guildhall in the City of London yesterday. “This is not a protest, it’s a rebellion. The social contract between the people and the state is broken,” she said. “We are in an active rebellion against the British government.”
Over the weekend XR’s police liaison team met with the Metropolitan Police for what they described as a “positive discussion”.
But they said that they had given away little information as to what the group has in store over the course of the two-week protest.
Paul Stephens, a member of the XR police liaison team and a former Met detective sergeant, said that on previous occasions when the group had told the police about their plans, they had met with more heavy-handed policing.
One activist, who had travelled to London from Cardiff, said this was the second XR protest she had attended. “I’m looking forward to getting arrested,” said Zoella Took, 22. “It’s the least I can do given the situation we are in. It’s inspirational to be among so many people from all different backgrounds, genders, ethnicities, who are fighting for the same thing. It gives me hope.”
The Metropolitan Police said a “significant” operation would be put in place to manage the protests over the busy bank holiday weekend but acknowledged the activists’ “important cause”.
Matt Twist, deputy assistant commissioner, said: “It is clear to us from reading and listening to their public announcements that Extinction Rebellion’s intention is to once again cause significant disruption to London and to London’s communities through acts of civil disobedience.
“There have been three previous extended periods of demonstrations by Extinction Rebellion in London. People going about their normal business saw bus routes being diverted or cancelled, significant roads closures, tubes and DLR [Docklands Light Railway] routes being disrupted by spontaneous demonstrations, and the abstraction of hundreds if not thousands of officers from their normal duties.
“Like everyone else, Extinction Rebellion have the right to assemble and the right to protest. However, these rights are qualified and are to be balanced against the rights of others. They do not have the right to cause serious disruption to London’s communities and prevent them going about their lawful business.
“Undoubtedly, an operation on this scale will impact our policing in communities across London. Every police officer committed to a large demonstration is a police officer abstracted away from their local borough and community. Each painstaking hour spent dealing with a protester who has committed criminal damage, glued or locked on to a road or business, is time spent away from the people of London, in the parts of London who need us most, dealing with knife crime, domestic abuse, violence.
“I want our police officers to be serving Londoners, fighting crime as well as bearing down on our number one priority: violence. It is frustrating that activity by Extinction Rebellion will hinder those efforts.”
The movement has gained support from celebrities such as the comedian and author Stephen Fry and actor Jerome Flynn.
Flynn, who starred in Game of Thrones, attended yesterday evening’s protest in which three activists scaled the Guildhall.
A crowd of around 200 people gathered as the trio sprayed red paint over the walls of the building and unfurled a banner reading “co-liberation — freedom together”.
Flynn said it was “more urgent than ever” for people to take a stand. “We’ve gotten used to certain systems that are life-destructive; we created them, we’ve become addicted to them and we know the world is burning as a result,” he said.
“It feels needed and more poignant and more urgent than ever to come together. It’s time to collaborate; there are so many things that are trying to polarise us and pull us apart.”

https://www.thetimes.com/world/asia/arti.title: Why I’m bailing out of China and heading into shipping
https://www.thetimes.com/world/asia/arti.text:
At what point do those who “know their own mind” turn into pig-headed fools? Put another way, when should we accept that we might be wrong?
Such philosophical musings have practical consequences for investors because they can involve substantial sums of money. I have just sold two shares I held for more than a decade and also got rid of a recent disappointment.
Vodafone (stock market ticker VOD), the telecommunications giant, kept me hanging on the line with inflation-busting income but non-existent capital growth until I sold at £1.17 in my summer clear-out. I first invested via a paper-based broker at, from memory, about £1.40 in the early noughties.
Its price exceeded £3.50 at the start of this century and I believed I was buying into a temporary dip. When that turned into a long-term downward trend, I dithered because I was reluctant to surrender its yield of more than 6 per cent.
Henderson Far East Income (HFEL) investment trust is an even higher yielder, paying 7.6 per cent. Reinvesting these dividends doubled investors’ capital in less than a decade but the share price never made much progress.
I bailed out when I noticed Henderson had increased its holdings in China to 17 per cent of the fund — plus another 22 per cent in Taiwan and 11 per cent in Hong Kong. As discussed here last year, I would rather not invest in a country accused of genocide by, among others, the American president Joe Biden. I also fear that the world’s two biggest economies are engaged in a cold war that could heat up suddenly, with Hong Kong and Taiwan potential flashpoints.
The same reasoning prompted me to sell Jupiter Emerging & Frontier Income (JEFI) when I noticed it now holds 20 per cent of its assets in Taiwan, 15 per cent in China and 7 per cent in Hong Kong. This share was performing well — I was 22 per cent up when I sold at £1 per share on Monday — but the past is not necessarily a guide to the future.
Tragic events unfolding in Afghanistan demonstrate how trends that were developing so slowly they were almost imperceptible can speed up so quickly that “little people” are powerless to act. So this small investor, who is becoming scared by the news from far-off places, has decided to keep more of his money closer to home.
European Assets Trust (EAT) gives me exposure to medium-sized and smaller businesses on the Continent. The shares are priced 5.9 per cent below their net asset value (NAV) and yield 5.6 per cent, according to the independent statisticians Morningstar. Critics do not like the fact that dividends are partly funded by capital growth, but when that comes from companies such as Nordic Semiconductor, the Norwegian Bluetooth technology specialist, that’s fine by me. I paid £1.45 per share on Monday.
It might prove too good to be true but I hope EAT’s asset allocation will continue to deliver decent dividends with capital growth while adding diversification to my continental blue chips. Among others, these include Adidas (ADS) the German sports goods maker and Nestlé (NESN) the Swiss food giant — both in my top 10 holdings — plus EssilorLuxottica (EL), the Franco-Italian group that makes a third of the world’s spectacle lenses and Heineken (HEIO) the Dutch brewer.
Even more excitement might be expected from the other high yielder I have bought for tax-efficient income from my Isa. When the world’s biggest container ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days in March it reminded me that 80 per cent of goods bought and sold internationally are transported by sea. Since then, the Ever Given has delivered her load to Felixstowe, Suffolk, and passed through the Suez Canal again last weekend on her way back to Asia.
Global trade is also returning to something like normality after the peak of the pandemic and the Baltic Dry Index (BDI) of international shipping has doubled since its low point last year. But the BDI remains less than half the peak it hit before the global financial crisis began in 2008, so there is scope for further recovery. Here and now, some shipping businesses pay shareholders to be patient.
That’s why I have bought into a little-known £323 million company called Tufton Oceanic Assets (SHIP) at $1.21 a share. It’s listed on the London Stock Exchange and yields income of 5.9 per cent. Tufton owns 21 second-hand ships of various sizes — excluding the Ever Given — while aiming for capital growth and rising income.
Shrewd observer Mick Gilligan, a partner at the stockbroker Killik, tells me: “Shipping is one of the most cyclical industrial sectors but the evidence suggests that we are in the early stages of what could be a sustained improvement in shipping rates.” Sachin Saggar, a director at the investment bank and broker Stifel, said: “When inflation and logistic concerns are growing we think the shipping sector offers protection and the potential to generate strong returns.”
Both European Assets Trust and Tufton give me stakes in global economic recovery but with less of the political risk that is rising in Asia. Sooner or later stock market rough and tumble teaches us all a degree of humility. But I hope this summer’s reshuffle pays off.
Shares in the Sheffield-based maker of “green hydrogen”, ITM Power, surged 20 per cent to trade at £4.73 after Kwasi Kwarteng, the Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy, switched on its electrolyser factory, the biggest in the world.
For anyone as dim as me about chemistry, it may be worth explaining that electrolysers can split water into its constituent molecules of hydrogen and oxygen using renewable power generated by solar and wind farms. This zero-carbon green hydrogen can then decarbonise industrial processes, transport and heating to reduce pollution and climate change.
So it’s a pity that ITM’s important step toward turning science fiction into commercial fact didn’t get anything like as much media coverage as Extinction Rebellion mucking about in London. Maybe Yorkshire is just too far away from most news desks.
It’s more than a decade since I first invested in ITM and, even after selling shares worth 50 per cent more than my original stake at £5.39 last January, this remains the sixth most valuable holding in my “forever fund”.
With stakes in Ecofin Global Utilities & Infrastructure (EGL), an investment trust whose biggest asset is a renewable electricity company; Gore Street Energy Storage (GSF), the batteries specialist that aims to smooth fluctuations in solar and wind power; Orsted (ORHE), the world’s biggest offshore wind farm operator; and the self-explanatory US Solar Fund (USFP), nearly a tenth of my life savings is now invested in renewable energy.
In however small a way, these businesses should help things change for the better and make my money matter. Whether they make money over the long term remains to be seen.
Read a full list of Ian Cowie’s “forever fund” at thesundaytimes.co.uk/cowieholdings

https://www.thetimes.com/article/kevin-m.title: Kevin McCloud on how homeowners can go green
https://www.thetimes.com/article/kevin-m.text:
The latest eco-innovation, about to be trialled in the attic of sustainability pioneer Kevin McCloud, is surprisingly low tech. The broadcaster, who has presented the Channel 4 series Grand Designs since it first aired in 1999, says, “What I’m going to do is put the insulation into big plastic sacks and roll them out like giant duvets across the floor, and turn the attic into a temporary winter-only insulated space, so the floors below get the benefit of that, and then in the spring, remove said insulation to make the attic more accessible.” Genius. Cold is seasonal so why not insulation?
The race to net zero will affect every area of our lives, and alter our homes. The problem is, nobody is quite sure how. The schedule is fixed — the UK is aiming at a 68 per cent reduction by 2030 and zero carbon emissions by 2050 — but the measures we are encouraged to embrace are subject to change. Homeowners need independent, experienced, farsighted advice when they weigh the pros and cons, and consider the likelihood of greener — and cheaper — options becoming available nearer the deadline. And McCloud, with two decades in the sustainability game, could be the green guru we need.
He has been assisting Richard Bacon — the MP for South Norfolk who drove the Right to Build act through parliament in 2015, and whose review into self-building as the key to greener communities was published yesterday (see panel) — but McCloud says he has no interest in entering the political debate.
“I was involved at the fringes of the last big green deal 12 years ago, the one that fell flat on its face. I’m not built for that,” he admits. “My job is to go out and stand in fields and meet people and tell stories.” He is a supporter of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, and a member of the Green Party, but says, “I can’t agree with violence. I’m not a member of Extinction Rebellion, nor would I be.”
What he has always been is an enthusiast. “I was certainly on the fringes of greenery — variegated. I think that came from a Methodist upbringing, non-conformist, always suspicious of what I was being told. When Grand Designs came along, I had been gardening organically for 15 years and playing around with technology.” Since the world has caught up with his views on environmentally friendly living, McCloud, the lifelong non-conformist, finds himself in the position of being Mr Mainstream.
When self-builders on Grand Designs superinsulate their projects, it hardly bears mentioning now, and air source heat pumps need no explanation. Nearly every build featured in the series incorporates mechanical ventilation and heat recovery. While that is the story at the top of the architect-designed new-build tree, lower down, McCloud says, there is much work to be done. “We produce such poor quality housing, some of the poorest in Europe, and some of the smallest homes and most expensive homes in Europe. They are really poorly built. Not because people intentionally build them badly but land is so expensive in the UK that house builders find it incredibly hard to make money building high quality so have to lower the quality to make stuff accessible.”
Only a fraction of new homes are constructed to the ultra energy-efficient Passivhaus standard. McCloud says that one way to achieve higher sustainability goals could be with more high-quality “custom builds” — factory-made eco-homes. “The vast majority of the custom builds are coming from Europe where custom build is the norm. You visit a show home and sit down and plan out your house, with a choice of windows, taps, carpets. One of the most interesting is a company called Dan Wood, who’ve come to the UK (dan-wood.co.uk). You can order, and in two to three months you got your finished home, tiled and decorated.”
At Grand Designs Live each year, new developments are exhibited in a mini show called Kevin’s Green Heroes. The next edition, at the NEC Birmingham from October 6-10, features one product that mixes limewash with graphene; another called Polywood; bioresins from plants mixed with wood fibres to make a material that can be as strong as steel; and a breathable, low-impact, low-carbon insulating material called Inno-Therm, made from old cotton denim jeans. McCloud remains curious about the cutting edge of green innovation, and also sings the praises of natural materials, such as cork, “It’s an insulator, it’s sustainable, it’s fungicidal, naturally antibacterial, it expands and contracts, it absorbs moisture and slowly releases it. It does all this high-tech stuff for you, and it’s just the bark of a tree.”
The list of eco-ideas we should treat with scepticism, according to McCloud, is long. Instead of building a wind turbine, which will be “labour and materials intensive; it’s not going to deliver you all your energy and in the end you’ll still have to rely on the grid”, he suggests “open up an account with Green Energy or Ecotricity because there is a good green electricity supply market now”.
The inside line on the hydrogen boiler? “Hydrogen, well it can come from water — which is very appealing, isn’t it? But when you examine the energy cost of producing the hydrogen and getting it through the pipes to the boilers, I think it works out as seven to nine times more carbon-intensive than just using electricity off the grid. What you need to do is look at the whole supply chain and realise the impact. It’s rather like running an electric car. When your electricity is produced by a coal-fired power station. It doesn’t really solve anything.”
In his new home, a period building, McCloud intends to embrace tried-and-tested heating technology. “I’m thinking, where I now live, I’ll replace the system I’ve got with a heat pump. People are saying “why are you doing that, Kevin, why aren’t you making something yourself, out of bits of old pipe or something?” I just want things to work! Most of the early adoption I’ve done, I’ve regretted. I once had a boiler that burnt old pallets and bits of lumber from building sites that were chipped. It would stop regularly because the company I bought the chips from had left in the old nails, screws and fixings. They would get stuck in the boiler and melt, and this amazingly complex boiler would revert to its mother tongue of German and bark orders at me that I couldn’t understand. I’ve been stung so many times now that I have learnt my lessons, and I’m happy to let other younger people to go and experiment — and I will film their travails.”
Times+ subscribers can register online for free to hear the whole of the interview,Times Earth: Sustainable Homes with Kevin McCloud, which will be broadcast on the evening of Thursday, September 23 as part of the Times+ Earth series. mytimesplus.co.uk
Boris Johnson has long described himself as a One Nation Tory. But the country is “in danger of becoming two nations”, according to the prime minister’s independent review on housing, released yesterday.
Britain will soon be “one nation in which a whole generation struggles to find somewhere to afford to live at all, while the other adds to its buy-to-let portfolio”, according to Richard Bacon, the Conservative MP and author of the report.
So how do we create more housing? Relying on volume housebuilders and their shoddily built estates has created a nation of Nimbys. The solution, it seems, is to build it ourselves. Make it easier to self-build and custom-build houses. So that “the people commission the houses they would like to see”, Bacon says. This model will create wider and more affordable options and tap into a “missing market”.
We need to be more like the Germans. In the UK about 13,000 homes a year are self-build or custom-build, about 8 per cent of total new-builds. In Germany the total is 55 per cent, according to the report, which has six recommendations for the government to adopt. These include providing serviced building plots (like a WeWork site for self-builders); building a Show Park to raise awareness (like a permanent Grand Designs Live); increase funding and loans to community groups to build more affordable schemes; encourage lenders to go easy on self-builders as their energy costs will be lower; make it easier for self-builders to get planning permission and ensure they follow design codes; and look at tax incentives. Power to the people.Hugh Graham
